facts.fact: Gravel is the most common substrate in freshwater aquaria. Grain sizes run from pea-sized down to 1–2 mm.
Gravel sold for aquaria is usually chemically inert, typically quartz or other lime-free minerals.
Substrates give beneficial bacteria a surface to grow on and are part of biological filtration, for example in undergravel filters and deep sand beds.

Calcium carbonate substrates such as shells, coral and coral sand raise hardness and pH. They suit hard-water cichlids and marine tanks but are poorly suited to most river fish, which are adapted to soft water.
Peat softens water by ion exchange and often stains it yellow or brown with tannins.
Leaf litter releases tannins that tint the water reddish and is used in blackwater biotopes. Some leaf material may be poisonous.
Richer layers such as potting soil, peat, vermiculite or clay can supply iron and trace elements to plant roots. Clay mixed into sand can add extra nutrients for plants.
Gravel gives plants a place to root, acts as a filter layer and is a place where fish lay eggs.
JBL says fine sand suits scavenging and burrowing fish, while medium and coarse gravel do not suit them.
JBL PlantSoil and ShrimpSoil have low carbonate hardness and soften the water. PlantSoil is loaded with nutrients for heavily planted tanks, and ShrimpSoil has no added nutrients.
Tropica Aquarium Soil Powder is a complete substrate that needs no other bottom layer. It has a 1–2 mm grain and lowers pH naturally.
According to Aquasabi, ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia is acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) and acidifies the water. Water changes with near-neutral water slowly push pH back toward neutral.
According to Aquasabi, alkaline tap water weakens the pH-lowering effect of ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia. For tap water around pH 8.0, the page recommends adding ADA 'be Soft' during water changes.
Seiryu stone can slightly raise hardness and pH. It suits livebearers or rainbowfish better than soft-water fish such as discus.
Some stones change water chemistry a lot over time, so test the water regularly when using mineral-rich rock.
Calcium carbonate rocks (limestone, marble, coral rock, calcite, seiryu stone) are unsuitable for soft-water planted tanks and Caridina shrimp tanks.
In the vinegar test, fizzing or bubbling on the rock shows calcium carbonate, which can raise GH and KH over time.
Pyrite ('fool's gold') has a brassy, metallic yellow lustre and cubic crystals. Do not use it, because it can release sulphuric acid and drop pH.
Metallic veins in a rock, green or blue (copper) or rust-red (iron oxide), are a reason to test it carefully or avoid it.
In a soak test, a rise in GH or KH, or a pH shift of more than 0.2–0.3 units, means the rock is leaching minerals.
Vinegar test: clean the rock thoroughly, put a few drops of white vinegar on its surface, and watch for fizzing.
Soak test: place the clean rock in RO or distilled water, measuring GH, KH and pH before adding it. Re-test at 48 hours, 1 week and 2 weeks.
Do the soak test in RO water rather than tap water, because the minerals already in tap water can hide leaching.
Scrub heavy rust deposits off a rock before testing it, because they may raise iron above what plants tolerate.
Spread sand, gravel or crushed rock 2–7 cm deep. A 2–3 cm nutrient soil layer can go underneath, but it must be kept very clean.
Use a brush to level the gravel and shape it as you like.
In tall tanks, stand large flat stones upright like a canyon. In low tanks, lay flat stones in horizontal or sloping layers.
Arrange stones so they make hiding places for small fish.
JBL says the substrate should be no thinner than 3–5 cm, and heavily planted tanks can use 6–8 cm. Banking it higher toward the back makes the tank look bigger.
Planted tanks should have a substrate at least 5 cm (2 in) deep.
Tropica's example uses an 8 cm layer of Aquarium Soil, thicker toward the rear glass.
Tropica: substrate volume in litres = length × width × layer depth (cm) ÷ 1000. A 90 × 60 cm tank with an 8 cm layer needs 43.2 L.
Tropica recommends changing 25–50% of the water at least twice a week for the first 4 weeks after setting up with Aquarium Soil.
JBL Manado Dark must be rinsed once under running water before use.
If the water goes cloudy after filling over ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia, remove the cloudy water and refill slowly, repeating if needed. Start the filter only once the water is clear.
Fill over ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia through a hose, aiming for about 25°C water, and add a chlorine neutralizer.
Aquasabi says to add fish and shrimp two to three weeks after planting a tank set up with ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia.
ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia leaches ammonium after setup. Above pH 7.0 this can turn into forms that are toxic to fish and shrimp.
When ADA Aqua Soil granules crumble and the bed becomes less permeable, blue-green algae may develop, and Aquasabi advises rebuilding the substrate.
Lava substrate has sharp edges, and bottom-dwelling fish can injure themselves on it. Sansibar sand and natural Manado have rounded grains.
Some aquarists prefer fine gravel (1–2 mm) because coarser grains trap debris.
Never clean rocks with soap or detergent, because the residues are toxic to fish.
Passing the vinegar test only shows there is no calcium carbonate. It does not prove the rock is inert, and it does not detect iron sulphides such as pyrite, which can oxidise later.
JBL Sansibar SNOW, WHITE, RED, DARK and GREY are not suitable over undergravel heating cables. Sansibar RIVER is.
Red Bee shrimp and Caridina japonica pick at ADA Aqua Soil granules, so a shrimp-only tank with exposed soil stays somewhat cloudy. Spreading foreground plants help.
JBL says soil substrates lose their benefits within two years at most and must be replaced. Sand, gravel and Manado need only regular siphoning.
Aquasabi says ADA Aqua Soil Amazonia lasts about two to three years. After that, add Multi Bottom or replace the top layer.
JBL Sansibar SNOW sand is 0.1–0.6 mm, the other Sansibar colours are 0.2–0.6 mm, and Sansibar RIVER is 0.8 mm.
Sand is often recommended for river stingrays (Potamotrygonidae), which bury themselves in fine substrate.
Betta splendens does best in a well-planted, shady tank with plenty of surface cover, such as floating plants (Salvinia, Riccia) and Cryptocoryne.
For bettas, small clay plant pots, lengths of plastic pipe or empty film canisters can serve as extra shelter. Driftwood is fine.
Dried leaf litter gives bettas cover and supports microbes that can feed fry. Tannins from decaying leaves are considered beneficial.
In the wild, the substrate in betta habitats ranges from leaf litter to mud, sand or deep sediment.
3 mm gravel is a popular choice for medium-sized tanks.
Vietnamese names: nền / chất nền = substrate; sỏi = gravel; cát = sand; phân nền = soil substrate; đá đập vụn = crushed rock; đất dinh dưỡng = nutrient soil layer.
Lava rock is called 'đá nham thạch' or 'đá núi lửa' in Vietnam. Vietnamese aquarium shops sell soil substrate, sand and gravel (phân nền, cát, sỏi).

Vietnamese betta keepers use 'sỏi màu' (coloured gravel), 'sỏi tự nhiên' (natural gravel), 'đá ở sông hồ' (river or lake stones), 'cây cảnh bằng lụa' (silk plants) and 'cây cảnh bằng nhựa dẻo' (plastic plants). 'Hoa huệ' in the translated article stands for peace lily (Spathiphyllum, Lan Ý / Bạch môn).
